evidence: Cic. Fam. 7.9.1: jam diū ignōrō quid agās
Ter. Hec. 84: ubi tē oblectāstī tam diū?
terms.comment: Jam diū with the present is “for a long time now”, as in Cicero’s jam diū ignōrō. Tam diū, so long; quam diū?, how long? (see how long?); diūtius, longer, any longer. Long ago is ōlim or jam prīdem.
When the time itself is named: post longum tempus, after a long time.

phrases.latin: jam diū ignōrō quid agās; nihil enim scrībis
phrases.english: I’ve had no idea for ages how you are; you never write

phrases.latin: Dīc mihi, Philōtis, ubi tē oblectāstī tam diū?
phrases.english: Tell me, Philotis, where have you been enjoying yourself all this time?

sources: Lewis & Short: diu · Lewis & Short: longus · Lewis & Short: tempus
